item: Core defects found by verifiers during wave 1 (not in the original tracker maps)
summary: Two defects in core paths were found while verifying other packages. (1) On the complete SQLite runtime a multi-document request applies only its first new or changed document: `kudurru apply -f three.yaml` on a standalone node creates the first record set and answers `unavailable: current writable serving generation unavailable` for the others, and needs one run per document; `kudurru apply -f a -f b -f c` and a nine-document `kudurru restore` on a new node behave the same way. Reproduced on the base commit 33ee04bc and on the forwarding lane's binary; evidence in .context/v020-final-20261110/evidence/DOCS-OPS/verify-r3-xmulti-lane01.log, verify-r3-xmulti-ha01.log and verify-r3-restore-ha01.log, and the script that produced them next to those logs (verify-r3-*.py / *.sh). Single-document commands work. No hosted test covers a multi-document apply of new documents on the complete SQLite runtime. (2) Commit `fix(dns): answer an upstream failure across a canonical commit` (cherry-picked from the qualification lane; find it with `git log --grep 'answer an upstream failure across a canonical commit'`) widened `retainedDNSResponse` in cmd/kudurru/serving_update_output.go so that an empty SERVFAIL with status servfail_upstream or timeout_upstream and an unattributed or failure origin is released for a query captured on a retired data generation. The verifier of that package found the released class broader than the commit says: it also covers refusals the node produces itself without contacting any upstream (the native-recursion capture refusal, a failed serving capture in Stage.Bind, indeterminate DNSSEC validation), and on a node whose default group is `mode: recursive` a cache-miss lookup in the 60 to 90 ms after every canonical commit now gets an immediate SERVFAIL with extended DNS error 23 (network error) although no upstream was contacted, where it previously got no answer and succeeded on the client's retry. Details and measurements: the verify:QUAL-CI result in the qualification lane journal, summarized in $SHARED/out/QUAL-CI/ledger.md and $SHARED/out/QUAL-CI/decision.md, logs under $SHARED/evidence/QUAL-CI/.
alreadyDone: Follower forwarding of multi-item requests was bounded and documented by the forwarding lane (decision rows in $SHARED/out/HA-FIX/decision.md, row 2 'Multi-item requests through an enrolled follower' and row 3 'Member command acknowledgment under the commit's own writer exclusion'). Those rows keep the original-source rule (capture once, never retarget) and report later items as `unavailable` when the follower's installed source changed. Read them before designing: the standalone and primary case below must stay consistent with them, and may require correcting what they and docs/deploy/sqlite-cluster.md section 4 and docs/deploy/sqlite-join.md say about running an apply again.

Single-document current commands on SQLite (objects, zone commands, domain commands, unblock decisions, migrations) are complete current commands with original-proof admission (tracker gates G01 to G03, dev-docs/milestones/v0.2/gaps.md lines 65-70).

remaining.title: A multi-document apply, batch delete or restore must apply every document in one run on the complete SQLite runtime
remaining.detail: Find why items after the first new or changed document of one request are refused with `unavailable: current writable serving generation unavailable` on a standalone or primary SQLite node (start from the POST /apply handler in internal/api, the object command write path internal/api/object_command_write.go, the current-command admission and source capture under cmd/kudurru/serving_*.go and internal/servinghttp, and the publication gate in internal/serving). The likely cause is that the request captures its writable serving generation once, the first item's commit retires that generation, and the next item starts before the new generation is published or is compared against the request's original capture. Design the smallest change that lets one request apply all of its documents while keeping every guard that exists for a reason: the original credential and source are still captured once and rechecked at each commit; a commit by anyone else between two items must still refuse the later items (no silent retargeting to foreign state); no refused or uncertain item is replayed; the request stays bounded by its original lifetime; per-item results keep their present shape (one result per document, earlier items stay committed). One principled option is to let item N+1 be admitted against exactly the generation that this request's own item N produced (an exact compare against the request's own commit receipt, waiting, within the request's lifetime, for that generation to be published), so that only the request's own commits can advance its source. Decide and record the rule. Cover POST /apply, POST /{kind}:batchDelete, the kind collection routes that take several documents if any, `kudurru restore`, and the same requests arriving through an enrolled follower (where the follower's installed source lags the primary: decide whether the follower can chain on the primary's receipts or must keep the documented partial result, and make docs/deploy/sqlite-cluster.md and docs/deploy/sqlite-join.md agree with each other and with the code; today they contradict each other about whether running the apply again through the follower helps). Check the Kubernetes driver too (it has no such gate, but prove multi-document apply there with envtest so both drivers have the test).
remaining.acceptance: dev-docs/milestones/v0.2/gaps.md line 110 (G21: no unexplained 501/503 remains in supported workflows) and README V2-OPS (apply/restore are core operations). Tests that fail before the fix: (a) mounted complete-SQLite runServe test through the real router and the real CLI client: one POST /apply with three new record sets creates all three in one request, they are served over DNS, and a second identical apply reports three `unchanged`; (b) `kudurru apply -f a -f b -f c` and a multi-document `kudurru restore` into a new node complete in one run; (c) POST /{kind}:batchDelete of several names deletes all in one request; (d) a foreign commit injected between two items (another credential's write, or a status/controller write that changes the admission-relevant source: say exactly which writes count as foreign) still refuses the later items with the documented key and applies nothing for them, and nothing is replayed; (e) the request's original lifetime still bounds the whole request; (f) a revoked or downgraded credential between items stops the later items; (g) the two-process enrolled test in test/e2e applies a multi-document file through the follower with the documented outcome; (h) envtest multi-document apply on the Kubernetes driver. Run the existing current-command, object, zone, migration and member-forward selections to show nothing regressed.

remaining.title: Narrow the retained SERVFAIL release across a canonical commit to failures of an upstream that was actually contacted, and settle what a recursive node answers in the window after a commit
remaining.detail: Reproduce the two problems the verifier reported for the commit `fix(dns): answer an upstream failure across a canonical commit`: (1) on a node whose default upstream group is `mode: recursive`, a cache-miss query in the tens of milliseconds after a canonical commit (for example creating an API token through the admin socket, or any object write) is answered SERVFAIL with extended DNS error 23 although no upstream was contacted; before that commit the query got no answer and the client's retry succeeded. A stub resolver that receives SERVFAIL from its only server reports a failure to the application, so every configuration commit now causes a short burst of user-visible failures on recursive nodes; (2) the released class includes every empty SERVFAIL with status servfail_upstream or timeout_upstream and origin unattributed or failure, which also covers refusals the node produces itself: the native-recursion capture refusal, a failed serving capture in Stage.Bind, and indeterminate DNSSEC validation. Decide and implement the right behavior. The better fix for (1) is probably at the cause: a query that arrives in the window after a commit should not be refused by a capture that only failed because the generation just changed; it should either complete on the retained generation, as forwarded answers do, or be captured on the new generation, within its own deadline. If that is too large, at minimum the retained release must be limited to failures where an upstream attempt was really made and failed or timed out (find or add the evidence on the pipeline response, without touching the hot path's allocation profile: the performance gates F20d and F63 are tight), and node-produced refusals must keep their previous disposition. Either way the forwarding case the original commit fixed must keep working: a client whose upstream failed or timed out across a commit still gets its SERVFAIL (TestUpstreamFailureAnsweredAcrossCommits and TestCentralQuerylogTwoNodes). Correct the wording of the commit's paragraph in docs/architecture/query-path.md to describe the final class exactly.
remaining.acceptance: Tests that fail before the fix: a mounted test of a recursive-mode node (the existing recursor test harness with a local stand-in root; see internal/recursor tests and cmd/kudurru anchor/recursion mounted tests) that issues cache-miss queries without pause around several canonical commits and requires every query to be answered correctly (NOERROR with the expected data) or, if you decide a refusal is unavoidable in some window, exactly the documented answer and never a network-error SERVFAIL for a query that contacted no upstream; unit rows in the retained-response guard test for each node-produced refusal class (capture refusal, Stage.Bind capture failure, indeterminate DNSSEC validation) showing they are not released as upstream failures; the two existing forwarding tests still pass. No change to benchmark-relevant allocation counts on the query path (run the existing allocation guard tests in internal/stages and internal/pipeline).

remaining.title: A primary zone can answer SERVFAIL (servfail_unsynced) for its own committed data in a window after a status write
remaining.detail: Found by the review of the query-log sink package and confirmed by its independent verifier: TestRunServeSQLiteCompletePrimaryUpdateRestart (cmd/kudurru/serve_mount_test.go:119) can fail with `mounted built-in query lost committed authority: {Name:dynamic.example. ... Rcode:SERVFAIL Status:servfail_unsynced ... Upstream:secondary:unavailable:example.` when its built-in queries arrive about one second into the first server run (1 of 8 with an injected 1000 ms pause, 0 of 8 with 450 ms and as committed). The sink package's fixer attributed the window to behavior that predates that package (its log $SHARED/evidence/OBS-FANOUT/fix-flake04.log); the verifier found that attribution supported but did not rerun the base reproduction (logs $SHARED/evidence/OBS-FANOUT/pv2-probe01.log and pv2-root-race01.log). Establish first, with a control on the base checkout /home/vercel-sandbox/kudurru/.context/wt/base-33ee04bc (read-only), whether the window exists at 33ee04bc. Then find the mechanism: which commit (the primary zone's status write, a serial advance, a publication swap) makes the authoritative stage report the zone as unsynced or route the name to an unavailable secondary source, for how long, and whether a real node answers SERVFAIL for a committed primary zone in that window. The design rule is that DNS keeps answering from last-good data across commits. If a real node can hit it, fix the cause (the answer must come from the committed zone or the retained generation, never a transient SERVFAIL). If only the test's ordering is at fault, make the test wait on an observable state, not a sleep, and say why a client cannot see the window. Do not relax the assertion. This is related to CORE-RETAINED-SERVFAIL (answers across a canonical commit): read that package's result first.
remaining.acceptance: A deterministic test that reproduces the mechanism and fails before the fix; TestRunServeSQLiteCompletePrimaryUpdateRestart passes 100 consecutive runs under race pinned to 2 CPUs with the pause probe at 0, 450, 1000 and 2000 ms (keep the probe as an overlay or an env-gated hook that is not committed); a mounted test that queries a primary zone without pause across at least 20 status writes and serial advances and never sees SERVFAIL; the authoritative, primary runtime and update selections pass; allocation guard tests on the query path unchanged.

recommendation: Fix CORE-APPLY-MULTI first: it breaks a core operator workflow (apply and restore) on the default deployment shape. Follow the existing original-proof patterns and record the multi-item rule as a decision; keep the forwarding lane's rows consistent with it. Then CORE-RETAINED-SERVFAIL, preferring the fix at the cause for recursive nodes.
sharedSeams: internal/api/apply.go and object_command_write.go (the forwarding lane is editing follower refusals and forwarding in neighboring files)
testInfra: Mounted complete-SQLite tests: cmd/kudurru TestRunServeSQLite* and the real-router CLI tests (cli_router_contract_test.go, generated_transport_test.go). Member forwarding: TestRootMemberObjectCommandActualHTTP, TestRootMemberForwardApplyKindRoutesAndBatchDelete. Two-process: KUDURRU_E2E=1 go test -race -run TestEnrolledClusterProcesses ./test/e2e (about 70 s each). Retained-response guard: cmd/kudurru serving_update_output_test.go; TestUpstreamFailureAnsweredAcrossCommits in test/e2e. All heavy runs go through the lock wrapper described in AGENT-BRIEF.md.
risks: The original-source rule exists to prevent a request from acting on state its caller never saw; any chaining rule must be an exact compare against the request's own receipts, not a relaxed check.
The query path's allocation and latency gates are tight; do not add per-query allocations.
The forwarding lane (wip/v020/ha) is concurrently changing follower refusals; keep edits in shared files small and local.
